title: Lifelong Athleticism

learn.summary: The end goal isn't a number on a bar — it's being the 80-year-old who gets off the floor without hands. Muscle mass declines roughly 3–8% per decade after 30 and faster after 60 (sarcopenia), but trained people push that curve decades to the right. From here the practice is simple: retest, play, balance, and never fully stop.

do: Put a recurring quarterly event in your calendar titled 'Retest baselines' — first occurrence within 90 days of your original tests.

children.title: Retesting

learn.summary: Every 8–12 weeks, rerun the original four: resting HR, timed mile, push-up max, sit-to-stand. Trends beat snapshots — a bad test day means nothing, a flat six-month trend means your program needs a change. Retests are also the honest antidote to both complacency and pointless program-hopping.

do: If it's been 8+ weeks since your baseline, retest all four numbers this week and write one sentence about what changed.

children.title: Balance Training

learn.summary: Falls are the leading cause of injury death in adults over 65, and balance is trainable at any age. The 10-second one-leg stand is a validated screen — in one large study, adults unable to hold it had markedly higher 7-year mortality. Practice costs nothing: single-leg stands while brushing teeth, heel-to-toe walking, and eventually eyes-closed holds.

do: Stand on one leg for the duration of brushing your teeth (switch legs halfway) every day this week; test your eyes-open max hold on day 7.

children.title: Sport Sampling

learn.summary: Gym training builds capacities; sport spends them joyfully and adds what the gym can't — reaction, agility, and the motivation of play. Adults who attach fitness to a game (pickleball, climbing, martial arts, swimming, dance) show far better long-term adherence than gym-only exercisers. Racket sports in particular associate with some of the largest longevity benefits in cohort studies.

do: Book one beginner session of a sport you've been curious about — an intro class, an open-play night, or a friend's invitation — within the next two weeks.

children.title: Training Through Age

learn.summary: The rules shift, not vanish: after 50, prioritize power (moving moderately heavy things fast — it declines quickest), keep protein at the higher 1.6–2.0 g/kg range, extend warm-ups, and expect recovery to take a day longer than it used to. Masters athletes in their 70s routinely hold muscle mass comparable to sedentary 40-year-olds. The worst program at any age is stopping.

do: Add one explosive-intent movement to this week's training — 3 sets of 5 fast sit-to-stands, medicine-ball throws, or brisk stair climbs — moving as quickly as you safely can.
